title: Stage 8 Maths — Practice Test 1
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Practice test
summary: A full end-of-Stage-8 maths test in Checkpoint style: Paper 1 (no calculator) and Paper 2 (calculator), 1 hour and 50 marks each, with full worked solutions and a mark scheme.

items: This is a full **end-of-Stage-8 practice test** in the style of the Cambridge Lower Secondary Progression Tests and Checkpoint. The Checkpoint test itself is taken at the **end of Stage 9**; this test checks your Stage 8 maths and gets you used to the same kind of questions.
**Paper 1:** 1 hour, 50 marks. You are **not** allowed to use a calculator.
**Paper 2:** 1 hour, 50 marks. You **may** use a calculator.
**Equipment:** pen, pencil, ruler, protractor, compasses (geometrical instruments) and tracing paper if you want it. A scientific calculator for Paper 2 only.
The marks for each part are shown, e.g. [2]. A [2] question usually needs working: show it, because a correct method can earn a mark even if the final answer is wrong.
You may write on paper first if you like, then type your answers. For questions that ask you to draw, copy the grid or number line onto paper.

**Marking:** answers you type as a number, a word or a choice are checked automatically. Written answers (explanations, working, drawings) you mark yourself at the end with the mark scheme shown for each question — be strict, like a real examiner.
Your score is a **practice score**, not an official Cambridge result. Use it to find the topics you need to revise.
Leave a short break between the papers if you want, but do each paper in one sitting with the timer running.

blocks.title: Stage 8 Maths — Practice Test 1
blocks.intro: Two papers, 1 hour each, 50 marks each. Paper 1: no calculator. Paper 2: calculator allowed. Have a pen, pencil, ruler, protractor, compasses and paper ready.

questions.q:
Question 1
Work out 20 − 3 × (2 + 4)^{2} ÷ 12
questions.e: Brackets first: 2 + 4 = 6. Then the index: 6^{2} = 36. Then × and ÷ from left to right: 3 × 36 = 108, 108 ÷ 12 = 9. Last, the subtraction: 20 − 9 = **11**. Common mistake: working 20 − 3 = 17 first.

questions.q:
Question 2
Which of these numbers is an integer but **not** a natural number?
questions.e: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, … Integers also include 0 and the negative whole numbers. −7 is a whole number, so it is an integer, but it is negative, so it is not a natural number. 7 is both; −7/2 and 0.7 are rational numbers but not integers. Answer **A (−7)**.

questions.ms: 1 mark: correct answer 3^{6} AND a correct explanation, e.g. 'the base stays 3, you only add the indices', 'he multiplied the 3s / bases', 'he should not multiply the bases'. Do not accept 3^{6} with no explanation, or 3^{8} (multiplying the indices).
questions.e: When you multiply powers of the **same base**, keep the base and **add** the indices: 3^{4} × 3^{2} = 3^{4+2} = **3^{6}**. Hassan wrongly multiplied the bases (3 × 3 = 9). Check: 3^{4} × 3^{2} = 81 × 9 = 729 = 3^{6}, but 9^{6} = 531 441.

questions.q: (a) Work out ∛(−64)
questions.e: (−4) × (−4) × (−4) = 16 × (−4) = −64, so ∛(−64) = **−4**. A negative number has a negative cube root.
questions.p: Question 4

questions.e: (−3)^{2} = (−3) × (−3) = 9 (a negative number squared is positive). ∛(−8) = −2 because (−2)^{3} = −8. So 9 + (−2) = **7**. Common mistake: (−3)^{2} = −9.
questions.p: Question 4

questions.q: (a) Work out 34 × 0.1
questions.e: Multiplying by 0.1 is the same as dividing by 10, so the digits move one place to the right: 34 × 0.1 = **3.4**.
questions.p: Question 5

questions.q: (b) Work out 2.7 ÷ 0.01
questions.e: Dividing by 0.01 is the same as multiplying by 100 (there are 100 hundredths in 1), so 2.7 ÷ 0.01 = **270**. Common mistake: 0.027 (dividing by 100 instead).
questions.p: Question 5

questions.q:
Question 6
Which fraction is equal to a **recurring** decimal?
questions.e: 3/8 = 0.375, 7/20 = 0.35 and 9/25 = 0.36 all stop (terminate). 5/6 = 0.8333… with the 3 repeating for ever. A fraction in its simplest form terminates only when the denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5; 6 = 2 × 3 has a factor 3, so 5/6 recurs. Answer **C**.

questions.q:
Question 7
Work out 4 1/5 − 1 2/3
Show your working. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.
questions.ms: 1 mark: correct method with a common denominator of 15, e.g. 63/15 − 25/15, or 3 + 3/15 − 10/15, or 4 3/15 − 1 10/15 (oe). 1 mark: 2 8/15 (cao). Accept 38/15 for the method mark only.
questions.e: Estimate first: about 4 − 1.5 = 2.5. Change to improper fractions: 4 1/5 = 21/5 = 63/15 and 1 2/3 = 5/3 = 25/15. Then 63/15 − 25/15 = 38/15 = **2 8/15**. Or: whole numbers 4 − 1 = 3, then 1/5 − 2/3 = 3/15 − 10/15 = −7/15, so 3 − 7/15 = 2 8/15. 2 8/15 ≈ 2.5, which matches the estimate.

questions.q:
(a) The baker has 84 chocolate biscuits and 120 date biscuits. She puts all of them into bags. Every bag has the same number of chocolate biscuits and the same number of date biscuits, and none are left over.
What is the **greatest** number of bags she can fill?
questions.e: This is the highest common factor of 84 and 120. 84 = 2^{2} × 3 × 7 and 120 = 2^{3} × 3 × 5. Common prime factors: 2^{2} × 3 = **12**. Check: 84 ÷ 12 = 7 and 120 ÷ 12 = 10, both whole numbers.
questions.p:
Question 8
A bakery in Heliopolis makes biscuits and bread.

questions.q: (b) How many date biscuits are in each bag?
questions.e: 120 ÷ 12 = **10** date biscuits (and 7 chocolate biscuits) in each bag. Follow through: 120 ÷ your answer to (a).
questions.p:
Question 8
A bakery in Heliopolis makes biscuits and bread.

questions.q:
(c) One batch of bread dough uses 2 3/4 kg of flour.
Work out how much flour the baker needs for 6 batches. Show your working.
questions.e: Estimate: 3 × 6 = 18 kg, so a bit less than 18. Method: 2 3/4 × 6 = (2 × 6) + (3/4 × 6) = 12 + 18/4 = 12 + 4 1/2 = **16 1/2 kg**. Or 11/4 × 6 = 66/4 = 16 1/2. Marks: 1 mark for a correct method (e.g. 12 + 18/4 or 66/4 seen); 1 mark for 16 1/2 or 16.5.

questions.q:
(e) She has 13.2 kg of biscuit dough. Each baking tray holds 0.4 kg of dough.
How many trays can she fill? Show your working.
questions.e: 13.2 ÷ 0.4: multiply both numbers by 10 so you divide by a whole number: 132 ÷ 4 = **33** trays. Estimate check: 13 ÷ 0.4 is about 32. Marks: 1 mark for 132 ÷ 4 (or an equivalent method); 1 mark for 33.

questions.q:
Question 9
Work out 0.25 × 37 × 4 without a calculator.
Show how you can change the order to make the calculation easier.
questions.ms: 1 mark: answer 37 with a method that groups 0.25 × 4 = 1 (e.g. 0.25 × 4 × 37 = 1 × 37). Do not accept 37 with no working.
questions.e: Multiplication can be done in any order (the commutative law): 0.25 × 37 × 4 = 0.25 × 4 × 37 = 1 × 37 = **37**.

questions.q:
Question 10
Which symbol makes this statement true?
−0.65  ☐  −2/3
questions.e: −2/3 = −0.666… . On a number line −0.65 is to the right of −0.666…, so it is the larger number: −0.65 **>** −2/3. Answer **B**. Common mistake: thinking −0.666… is bigger because 0.666 > 0.65 — with negative numbers the order is reversed.

questions.q:
(a) The total cost of the trip is E£48 652.
Round E£48 652 to 2 significant figures.
questions.e: The first two significant figures are 4 and 8 (48 thousand). The next digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so round up: **49 000**. Common mistake: 48 or 49 (you must keep the place value).
questions.p:
Question 11
Year 8 students from a school in Cairo go on a trip to Luxor.

questions.q:
(b) The ratio of students to teachers on the trip is 15 : 2. There are 68 people altogether.
How many teachers are on the trip?
questions.e: 15 + 2 = 17 parts. 68 ÷ 17 = 4 people in each part. Teachers = 2 × 4 = **8** (students = 15 × 4 = 60; 60 + 8 = 68 ✓).
questions.p:
Question 11
Year 8 students from a school in Cairo go on a trip to Luxor.

questions.q:
(c) The group spends 45 minutes at a museum and 2 hours at the Karnak temples.
Write the ratio 45 minutes : 2 hours in its simplest form.
questions.e: Use the same units first: 2 hours = 120 minutes. 45 : 120. The HCF of 45 and 120 is 15, so divide both by 15: **3 : 8**. Common mistake: 45 : 2 (different units).
questions.p:

questions.q:

questions.q:
Question 12
Which of these is a **formula**?
questions.e: A formula connects two or more letters (variables) that stand for quantities, so you can work out one from the others: P = 2l + 2w gives the perimeter of a rectangle. 3x + 7 is an expression (no equals sign); 2x + 5 = 11 is an equation (true for one value, x = 3); 4n − 1 > 6 is an inequality. Answer **D**.

questions.q: (a) Expand  4x(3x − 2)
questions.e: Multiply each term in the bracket by 4x: 4x × 3x = 12x^{2} and 4x × (−2) = −8x. Answer **12x^{2} − 8x**. Common mistake: 12x − 8x or 12x^{2} − 2.
questions.p: Question 13

questions.q: (b) Factorise completely  8a^{2} + 12a
questions.ms: 2 marks: 4a(2a + 3). 1 mark: a correct partial factorisation, e.g. 2a(4a + 6), 4(2a^{2} + 3a) or a(8a + 12).
questions.e: The HCF of 8a^{2} and 12a: numbers HCF(8, 12) = 4; letters a^{2} and a have a in common. So the HCF is 4a. 8a^{2} ÷ 4a = 2a and 12a ÷ 4a = 3. Answer **4a(2a + 3)**. Check by expanding: 4a × 2a + 4a × 3 = 8a^{2} + 12a ✓. 'Completely' means nothing more can be taken out of the bracket.
questions.p: Question 13

questions.q:
Question 14
Solve  5x − 7 = 2x + 11
Show your working.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a correct first step collecting terms, e.g. 3x − 7 = 11 or 3x = 18 or 5x = 2x + 18. 1 mark: x = 6.
questions.e: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 7 = 11. Add 7 to both sides: 3x = 18. Divide by 3: **x = 6**. Check: 5 × 6 − 7 = 23 and 2 × 6 + 11 = 23 ✓.

questions.q:
Question 15
Show the inequality  −2 < x ≤ 3  on the number line. (Copy the number line onto paper.)
questions.ms: 1 mark: open (empty) circle at −2, closed (filled) circle at 3, and a line joining them. Do not award if the circles are the wrong way round.
questions.e: x is **greater than** −2 (−2 itself is not included) → open circle at −2. x is **less than or equal to** 3 (3 is included) → filled circle at 3. Join the circles with a straight line.

questions.q: (a) Find an expression for the nth term of the sequence.
questions.e: The terms go down by 3 each time, so the nth term starts with −3n. When n = 1, −3n = −3, and you need 7, so add 10: **10 − 3n** (or −3n + 10). Check: n = 2 gives 10 − 6 = 4 ✓. Marks: 1 mark for −3n + c (any c, or 'goes down by 3' used correctly); 2 marks for 10 − 3n.
questions.p:
Question 16
Here is a sequence:  7,  4,  1,  −2,  …

questions.q: (b) Is −50 a term in this sequence? Show how you decide.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 'Yes' with a correct reason, e.g. solving 10 − 3n = −50 to get n = 20 (a whole number), or saying −50 is the 20th term. Follow through from an incorrect nth term in (a) if the method is correct.
questions.e: Solve 10 − 3n = −50: −3n = −60, so n = 20. n is a whole number, so **yes**, −50 is the 20th term. (If n had come out as a decimal, the number would not be in the sequence.)
questions.p:
Question 16
Here is a sequence:  7,  4,  1,  −2,  …

questions.q:
Question 17
Here is a function machine.
input → × 4 → − 3 → output
The output is 25. Work out the input.
questions.e: Use the inverse operations in reverse order: 25 + 3 = 28, then 28 ÷ 4 = **7**. Check: 7 × 4 − 3 = 25 ✓. Common mistake: 25 ÷ 4 + 3.

questions.q:
Question 18
Nour says, "A rhombus is always a square."
Is Nour correct? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 'No' with a correct reason, e.g. a rhombus does not have to have right angles; a square is a special rhombus (but not the other way round); a counter-example such as a rhombus with angles 60° and 120°. Do not accept 'No' with no reason.
questions.e: **No.** A rhombus has four equal sides, but its angles do not have to be 90°. A square has four equal sides **and** four right angles, so every square is a rhombus, but not every rhombus is a square. One counter-example (a rhombus with angles 70° and 110°) is enough to show Nour is wrong.

questions.q:
Question 19
Work out the area of this trapezium. Show your working.
questions.e: Area of a trapezium = ½ × (a + b) × h, where a and b are the parallel sides. ½ × (7 + 11) × 6 = ½ × 18 × 6 = 9 × 6 = **54 cm^{2}**. Marks: 1 mark for ½ × (7 + 11) × 6 or 18 × 3 seen; 1 mark for 54. Common mistake: using the sloping side, or forgetting the ½ (108).

questions.q:
Question 21
Amir uses a ruler and compasses. He draws arcs with the same radius from A and from B, then a straight line through the points where the arcs cross.
What has he constructed?

questions.e: Parallel lines have the same gradient. In y = mx + c the gradient is m, so we need m = 3: **y = 3x + 4** (answer **B**). y = −3x − 2 has gradient −3 (it slopes the other way) and y = x − 2 only shares the y-intercept.

questions.q:
(a) Ravi says, "A regular polygon with rotational symmetry of order 9 has 9 lines of symmetry and 9 sides."
Is Ravi correct? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 'Yes' with a reason, e.g. for a regular polygon the number of sides = number of lines of symmetry = order of rotational symmetry; it is a regular nonagon (9 sides) with 9 lines of symmetry.
questions.e: **Yes.** In a regular polygon, the number of sides, the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry are all the same. Order 9 means it is a regular nonagon: 9 sides and 9 lines of symmetry.
questions.p: Question 9

questions.q:
(b) A 3D shape has 12 vertices and 18 edges.
Use Euler's formula to work out the number of faces.
questions.e: Euler's formula: F + V − E = 2. F + 12 − 18 = 2, so F − 6 = 2 and **F = 8**. (A hexagonal prism has 12 vertices, 18 edges and 8 faces.)
questions.p: Question 9

(c) The plan (top view) of a solid is a circle. The front elevation is a rectangle.
Name the solid.
questions.e: From above you see a circle; from the front you see a rectangle. The solid is a **cylinder**. (A cone would have a triangle as its front elevation; a sphere would show a circle from every side.)

questions.q:
(d) Laila wants to know what all 600 students in the school think of the science fair. She asks the 30 students in her own science club.
Give **one** reason why this may not be a good sample.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a valid reason, e.g. the sample is biased / not representative because science-club students probably like science more than other students; only one group is asked; it is not random; 30 out of 600 is a small sample (accept). Do not accept 'it is unfair' with no explanation.
questions.e: The science club is not **representative** of the whole school: its members probably like science more than most students, so the results are likely to be **biased**. A better method is a random sample of students from every year group.

questions.q:
(e) Classes 8A and 8B took the same science quiz, marked out of 20.
Class | Mean | Range
8A | 14.2 | 6
8B | 12.8 | 15
Compare the scores of the two classes. Write **two** comparisons.
questions.ms: 1 mark: comparing averages in context, e.g. 8A did better on average because their mean is higher (14.2 > 12.8). 1 mark: comparing spread in context, e.g. 8A's scores were more consistent / less spread out because their range is smaller (6 < 15). Do not accept just quoting the numbers without saying what they mean.
questions.e: 1. **Average:** 8A's mean (14.2) is higher than 8B's (12.8), so on average 8A scored better. 2. **Spread:** 8A's range (6) is smaller than 8B's (15), so 8A's scores were more consistent; 8B's scores were more spread out. Always compare one average and one measure of spread, and say what they mean.

questions.q: (a) Write down the experimental probability that the spinner lands on red.
questions.e: Experimental probability = number of times red ÷ number of trials = 62 ÷ 200 = **0.31** (or 31/100).
questions.p:
Question 11
Omar has a spinner with four equal sections coloured red, blue, green and yellow. He spins it 200 times. It lands on red 62 times.

questions.q:
(b) Omar says, "The spinner is biased towards red."
Use the theoretical probability to comment on what Omar says.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a comment that compares with the theoretical probability 0.25 (or 50 out of 200), e.g. 'If fair, red should come up about 50 times; 62 is a lot more, so Omar could be right' or 'He may be right, but he should do more trials to be sure'. Must mention 0.25, 1/4 or 50.
questions.e: If the spinner is fair, P(red) = 1/4 = 0.25, so in 200 spins you would expect about 0.25 × 200 = 50 reds. Omar got 62, which is quite a lot more, so the spinner **may be biased** towards red. Experimental results always vary, so to be more sure he should do many more spins.

questions.q: (c) Omar spins the same spinner 500 times. Use his experimental probability to estimate how many times it lands on red.
questions.e: Expected number = probability × number of trials = 0.31 × 500 = **155**.

Question 12
Solve the equation  (3x − 1)/4 = x − 2
Show your working.
questions.ms: 1 mark: correct removal of the fraction, 3x − 1 = 4(x − 2) or 3x − 1 = 4x − 8. 1 mark: x = 7.
questions.e: Multiply both sides by 4: 3x − 1 = 4(x − 2) = 4x − 8. Subtract 3x from both sides: −1 = x − 8. Add 8: **x = 7**. Check: (3 × 7 − 1)/4 = 20/4 = 5 and 7 − 2 = 5 ✓.
